1.definition: The youngest son of Taejo and his favored crown prince, backed by the queen and by Jeong Do-jeon. His selection over his older, battle-tested half-brothers triggered the First Strife of Princes in 1398, in which Yi Bang-won had him killed.

A Korean idiom — literally "messenger to Hamheung" — meaning a person sent on an errand from which they never return. It comes from the story of the retired Taejo executing envoys his son sent to his refuge at Hamheung.
Shia religious scholars imported from Jabal Amil in present-day Lebanon, brought in to staff and teach the new Shia state religion of Safavid Iran, which had previously been majority Sunni.

2.matchText: Korean is a member of the Koreanic language family

2.definition: One of Sejong's two leading frontier generals, charged with the northwest. While Kim Jong-seo secured the northeast, Choe Yun-deok drove the Jurchen back across the Yalu and helped establish the Four Districts that fixed the Korea–China border.

A line of four military districts (the Sagun) planted along the upper Yalu River in the 1430s–1440s to garrison the territory Sejong's generals had cleared of Jurchen tribes. Together with the Six Forts on the Tumen, they fixed Korea's northern frontier roughly where it still runs today.

"Songs of the Moon Reflected in a Thousand Rivers," a Buddhist verse cycle composed by Sejong himself in the new Hangul script — among the earliest literary works written in the alphabet and a sign the king meant his invention to be used at the highest level, not just by commoners.

3.definition: The entrenched establishment faction of early-Joseon politics — the families of officials who had earned land and titles as "merit subjects" for backing the dynasty's founders, and who then dug in to keep their wealth and power against the rising reformist Sarim scholars.

An emergency package of modernizing decrees pushed through in 1894–1896 under Japanese pressure, named for the gabo year in the sexagenary cycle. They abolished the yangban–commoner class system, ended the gwageo exam, and outlawed slavery on paper — formally dissolving the five-hundred-year-old Joseon social order, even if the changes took decades to bite in practice.

A younger Joseon Neo-Confucian scholar (1527–1572) who carried on a decade-long, exquisitely written philosophical correspondence with the elder Yi Hwang over the metaphysics of the four moral feelings and seven emotions — the Four-Seven Debate. He argued that principle (li) and material force (gi) were not cleanly separable, against Toegye's more dualist view.

A landmark Korean Neo-Confucian controversy (sa-chil ron) over whether the four moral feelings and the seven natural emotions arise from principle (li), material force (gi), or both. Conducted as a sustained letter exchange between Yi Hwang and Gi Dae-seung, it set the philosophical fault lines that later hardened into Joseon's rival political factions.

4.definition: The Joseon dynasty's capital, founded in 1394 on the Han River and the site of modern Seoul (also called Hanseong). Its palaces were burned during the Imjin War's panicked 1592 evacuation.

5.definition: The "Reject Peace" faction at the Joseon court during the 1636 Manchu siege of Namhansanseong — hard-line Confucian officials who urged King Injo to keep fighting the Qing regardless of the cost, rather than submit to barbarian terms.

The "Accept Peace" faction at the besieged Joseon court in 1636 — pragmatic officials who argued for immediate surrender to the Qing to spare Korea worse devastation, against the hard-line Cheokhwapa.

The "Altar of Great Recompense," a shrine built inside the Joseon royal palace to perform annual sacrifices honoring the Ming Wanli Emperor, who had sent troops to rescue Korea in the Imjin War — a centerpiece of the post-1637 ideology that the fallen Ming, not the Qing, remained China's rightful sovereign.

The "Japan House," a tightly controlled trading enclave at Busan where a small number of Tsushima-clan Japanese merchants were permitted to live and trade — the only authorized Japanese presence in Joseon Korea during its long isolation.

The Sparrowhawk, a Dutch East India Company yacht bound from Batavia to Nagasaki that was driven off course by a typhoon and wrecked on Jeju Island in 1653, stranding the 36 survivors — including Hendrick Hamel — in Korea for thirteen years.

6.definition: "True-view landscape" — a Korean painting style, pioneered in the eighteenth century by Jeong Seon, that depicted real Korean mountains and scenery instead of the imagined Chinese landscapes that yangban convention demanded.

The treatise by the Silhak scholar Hong Dae-yong arguing that the earth rotates on its axis once a day and speculating about intelligent life on other planets — a strikingly bold leap in pre-telescopic Korean cosmology.

The Chinese-born Catholic priest (Korean name Ju Mun-mo, Chinese Zhou Wenmo) who slipped secretly into Joseon in 1795 to minister to a Korean church that lay converts had already organized for over a decade; he was executed in the Sinyu Persecution of 1801.

The Chinese-born priest sent to Joseon at the request of Korean lay Catholics, arriving covertly in 1795 — the first ordained clergyman to serve the self-founded Korean church. He was put to death in the 1801 persecution.

One of the construction innovations behind Hwaseong Fortress: uniform bricks fired in kilns built on-site rather than hauled from distant production centers, which sped the work and kept quality consistent.

The Hwaseong project's meticulous record-keeping, which logged every brick, beam, and stone in a construction manual (the Hwaseong Seongyeokuigwe) so complete that twentieth-century restorers used it to rebuild damaged sections faithfully.
Modeled on Ming and Qing China — the continental template of Confucian governance, the civil-service examination, script, and court ritual that Joseon Korea adopted and adapted.

7.definition: A senior Joseon official whose 1575 feud with Kim Hyo-won over a censorate appointment split the court into the Westerners and Easterners — the founding fracture of Joseon factional politics. His house in the western quarter of Hanyang gave the Westerner faction its name.
The Joseon official on the other side of the 1575 censorate quarrel with Sim Ui-gyeom. His house in the eastern quarter of the capital gave the Easterner faction its name.

The more hardline wing the Northerner faction split into around the 1610s, during the reign of Gwanghaegun. The label, like all the Joseon faction names, marked a network of intermarried scholar-officials rather than a policy platform.
The more moderate wing produced when the Northerner faction divided around the 1610s, the counterpart to the Greater Northerners.

The first Yesong ritual controversy, erupting in 1659 over how long the dowager queen should mourn the dead King Hyojong — a dispute that turned the technical mourning code into a fight over the legitimacy of the royal succession. The Westerner position (one year) won, and Southerner officials were exiled.
The second Yesong ritual controversy, in 1674, over the mourning owed to Hyojong's dead queen. This time the Southerner position prevailed; Westerner officials were exiled and several executed.

King Yeongjo's "impartiality" policy: appoint officials from the Old Doctrine and Young Doctrine factions in roughly equal numbers and build cross-factional cabinets, so as to break the all-or-nothing pattern of purge politics. It gave Joseon its longest stretch of court stability since the founding generations.

A series of conflicts (1775–1819) by which the British East India Company broke the Maratha Confederacy and completed its conquest of the Indian subcontinent. The final war ended in 1818 — the same era Joseon was paralyzed by Sedo politics.

A small county in the northwestern province of Pyeongan where Hong Gyeong-rae raised his rebellion in December 1811. The revolt spread rapidly across the discriminated-against northwest before being crushed at Jeongju the following spring.

Literally "in-law clan politics": the nineteenth-century system in which real power over Joseon was held not by a string of child or weak kings but by the maternal or wife's families of the throne — chiefly the Andong Kim and Pungyang Jo clans — who ran the state as a private patronage racket and hollowed out its capacity to face the modern world.

8.matchText: Korea would be a Japanese colony

8.definition: A Korean newspaper editor of the Korean Empire period whose 1905 editorial "I Wail Bitterly Today," lamenting the signing of the Eulsa Treaty, became one of the most famous protests against Japanese encroachment.

The "Outer Royal Library" on Ganghwa Island, a branch of the Joseon royal archive that held state documents and royal manuscripts; French marines burned it in 1866 and looted 297 royal volumes, which were not repatriated to Korea until 2011.

The United States and its citizens, a rising Pacific power that pressed Joseon to open its ports in the late nineteenth century and later, by the Taft-Katsura understanding, tacitly conceded Korea to Japanese control.
